description: Oba Femi, born Isaac Odugbesan on 22 April 1998 in Lagos, Nigeria, is a Nigerian professional wrestler signed to WWE, where he performs on Raw. A champion shot putter at the University of Lagos, Middle Tennessee State and the University of Alabama, where he won Southeastern Conference indoor titles in 2021 and 2022, he joined WWE through its Next In Line programme in 2021 with no prior wrestling experience. In NXT he won the 2023 Breakout Tournament, held the North American Championship for a record 273 days, and twice held the NXT Championship. Called up in January 2026 after vacating the NXT title undefeated, he entered the Royal Rumble first, beat Brock Lesnar at WrestleMania 42 and again inside Hell in a Cell at SummerSlam, and won the 2026 King of the Ring tournament. In October 2026 he remained an active Raw headliner, defeating Bronson Reed at Money in the Bank and rejecting Paul Heyman's overtures on the 12 October Raw.

name: Otis Boykin
description: Otis Boykin (1920-1982): Dallas-born inventor whose improved electrical resistors - including a 1959 wire precision resistor and a 1961 improved resistor (U.S. Patent 2,972,726) - made consumer electronics, IBM computers, guided missiles, and artificial cardiac pacemakers cheaper and more reliable. Valedictorian of Dallas's Booker T. Washington High School (1938); Fisk University (1941); lab assistant at Majestic Radio and TV Corp testing automatic aircraft controls; research engineer at P.J. Nilsen Research Labs; established Boykin-Fruth, Inc. with Hal Fruth; private consultant 1964-1982 for American and Paris firms. Held more than two dozen U.S. patents, including a burglar-proof cash register and a chemical air filter. Died of heart failure in Chicago, March 1, 1982. Inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame, 2014.

name: Ossie Davis
description: Ossie Davis (born Raiford Chatman Davis, December 18, 1917, in Cogdell, Georgia; died February 4, 2005, in Miami Beach, Florida) was an actor, playwright, director and social activist central to twentieth-century African American theatre and film. Raised in Waycross, Georgia, he attended Howard University for three years before leaving for New York, where he joined Harlem's Rose McClendon Players. After Army service in World War II he made his Broadway debut in Jeb in 1946, where he met Ruby Dee, whom he married in 1948; their artistic partnership became one of the American stage's most distinguished. Davis took over the role of Walter Lee Younger in A Raisin in the Sun, wrote the play Purlie Victorious (1961), and directed films including Cotton Comes to Harlem (1970). He and Dee served as master and mistress of ceremonies for the 1963 March on Washington, and he spoke at the funerals of both Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. Late in his career he appeared in Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing and Malcolm X. The couple jointly received the National Medal of Arts in 1995 and a Kennedy Center Honor in 2004.

name: Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life
description: Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life (1923–1949) was the official journal of the National Urban League, founded in New York in 1923 and, with the NAACP's Crisis, one of the two most influential African American periodicals of the first half of the twentieth century. Its founding editor was the sociologist Charles S. Johnson, who edited it from 1923 to 1928 and made it a Harlem Renaissance institution: beginning in 1924 Johnson ran literary contests — the first drew 732 entries — whose prizewinners included Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Countee Cullen, Sterling A. Brown, and Arna Bontemps, and the journal carried regular columns by Gwendolyn B. Bennett ('The Ebony Flute') and Cullen ('The Dark Tower'), with illustration by Aaron Douglas and Winold Reiss. Elmer Anderson Carter, who succeeded Johnson in 1928, turned its emphasis toward economics, labor, and politics while it continued to publish literature and art alongside social-science research on Black employment, migration, and city life. It ceased publication in 1949.

name: Ownership Change
description: Ownership or control changes - bankruptcy sales, corporate acquisitions, strategy pivots - that endanger or erase Black cultural holdings. Corporate-held Black memory is revocable memory. Documented cases: BET Digital removed its written news archive from BET.com in September 2026 in a video-first pivot (the Internet Archive then released 199,000+ of the removed articles); Paramount scrubbed decades of music news from MTV's website in 2024; Johnson Publishing Company's 2019 Chapter 7 bankruptcy turned the Ebony/Jet archive into bankruptcy assets auctioned for $30 million.

name: Obsolete Formats

name: Ovie Carter and Bob Black Negative Archives
description: The Ovie Carter and Bob Black Negative Archives are the personal negative archives of two octogenarian Black Chicago photojournalists. Ovie Carter worked at the Chicago Tribune from 1969 to 2004 and shared the 1975 Pulitzer Prize; Bob Black worked at the Chicago Defender from 1965 and at the Chicago Sun-Times from 1968 to 2006. Documentary footage in 'Voices in the Mirror' shows Carter examining negatives, indicating personal holdings. CTL's preservation research found no archive-transfer or finding-aid announcement for either man's negatives: their disposition is not publicly documented, and no succession is documented. The preservation package treats the two archives, held by photographers in their eighties, as the mortality-driven preservation risk in its purest form.

name: Oscar Micheaux Film Elements
description: Surviving elements of Oscar Micheaux's 44 features (1918-1940s): around 80 percent of the films are lost; only three silent features survive - Within Our Gates (1920), The Symbol of the Unconquered (1920), and Body and Soul (1925) - plus a handful of sound titles, several as single incomplete or reconstructed prints scattered across archives and private hands. Body and Soul (1925), which gave Paul Robeson his first film role, is the most complete surviving silent title; the Library of Congress placed it in the National Film Registry in 2019.

description: Off The Street Club is a youth organization in West Garfield Park, Chicago, founded in 1900 — by the organization's own account — and operating continuously into the present. It works as a youth safe-space and development club for West Side youth, offering athletics, tutoring, mentoring, arts programming, and camp. CultureTechLens's institutional research keeps the club for its longevity finding while flagging two cautions: it was founded in 1900, before its neighborhood was Black, and its current governance and funding are unverified in the research record.

name: Overcrowded segregated schooling (double shifts)
description: Chicago's Black Belt schools running double (two four-hour) shifts per day to handle enrollment surges from the Great Migration, with vocational tracking and stark resource gaps versus white schools. Between 1930 and 1940 the combined enrollment of 24 Bronzeville schools rose 65%; the district answered with 'doubleshift' schedules - Black students attended only part of the day - to preserve segregation. Superintendent Benjamin Willis (1953-1966) added 'Willis Wagons' portable trailers for Black students rather than sending them to under-capacity white schools. Over 200,000 students walked out in the 1963 Chicago school boycott over these conditions.

name: Obama Presidential Center
description: The Obama Presidential Center is the Obama Foundation's presidential center and civic campus in Jackson Park, on Chicago's South Side: a 19.3-acre complex of a museum, a forum, a branch of the Chicago Public Library, and the Home Court athletic center, set in gardens around the John Lewis Plaza. Washington Park was weighed for the site before the Foundation selected Jackson Park. The center broke ground on September 28, 2021, was dedicated on June 18, 2026, and opened to the public the next day — Juneteenth, June 19, 2026. Its museum, anchored by a 225-foot tower, traces American democracy, the civil rights movement, and the Obama presidency. Unlike the presidential libraries administered by the National Archives, the center is a private foundation campus and does not house the federal presidential archives. CultureTechLens research followed the center's contested siting in the Jackson Park dossier for a decade before it opened.

name: Otis Redding
description: Otis Redding (September 9, 1941 – December 10, 1967) was a Georgia-born soul singer whose five years of recording set the standard for Southern soul. Raised in Macon, he began recording for Stax’s Volt label in Memphis in 1962 with “These Arms of Mine,” and rose through albums including Otis Blue (1965), ballads such as “I’ve Been Loving You Too Long,” and a June 1967 Monterey Pop performance that carried him to rock audiences. On December 10, 1967, the plane carrying Redding and most of the Bar-Kays crashed into Lake Monona near Madison, Wisconsin; he was 26. Weeks later “(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay,” recorded days before his death, topped the Billboard Hot 100 for four weeks — the first posthumous number one in American chart history. He entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989 and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.

name: Otis Blue: Otis Redding Sings Soul
description: Otis Blue: Otis Redding Sings Soul is Otis Redding’s third studio album, released September 15, 1965 on Volt Records. All but one of its eleven tracks were recorded within a single 24-hour stretch, July 9–10, 1965, at Stax’s Memphis studio, with Booker T. & the M.G.’s, horn players from the Mar-Keys and the Memphis Horns, and Isaac Hayes at the piano behind him. Three songs are Redding’s own — “Ole Man Trouble,” “Respect,” and “I’ve Been Loving You Too Long” — and three are by Sam Cooke, who had died the previous December; the rest remake current hits, including the Rolling Stones’ “Satisfaction,” as Southern soul. The album became Redding’s first to top Billboard’s R&B albums chart, reached number six on the UK Albums Chart, and placed at number 78 on Rolling Stone’s 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums.

name: Omah Lay
description: Omah Lay, born Omah Stanley Didia on May 19, 1997, in Port Harcourt, Nigeria, is a singer and songwriter whose melancholic, melody-led take on Afrobeats made him one of the genre's defining new voices of the 2020s. Music runs in the family: his grandfather played for the highlife singer Celestine Ukwu. His debut EP Get Layd (2020) reached number one on Nigerian Apple Music, and its track 'Bad Influence' was the most-streamed Nigerian song on Apple Music at the end of 2020. A second EP, What Have We Done (2020), a Next Rated win at the 14th Headies, the Justin Bieber collaboration 'Attention' (2022), and his debut album Boy Alone (2022) followed. His second album, Clarity of Mind, arrived April 3, 2026 — the release CultureTechLens's Short documents, staged here to close the reverse gap.

name: Oak Woods Cemetery
description: Oak Woods Cemetery is a large Chicago cemetery at 1035 East 67th Street in the Greater Grand Crossing area of the South Side. It was chartered on February 12, 1853, covers 183 acres, and was designed by landscape architect Adolph Strauch as a landscape-lawn cemetery; sources differ on the first burials, giving 1860 in the cemetery's history and 1865 in Chicago Sun-Times reporting, and this record carries both dates rather than blending them. Oak Woods is the burial place of Chicago mayor Harold Washington, the city's first Black mayor; of anti-lynching journalist Ida B. Wells; of Olympic champion Jesse Owens; and of other prominent figures including Enrico Fermi and Cap Anson. The cemetery also holds the Confederate Mound, the mass grave and memorial for Confederate prisoners of war who died at Camp Douglas and were reburied here after the Civil War; its monument was dedicated in 1895. In September 1963, following protests, Oak Woods ended its racial segregation policy. It is a peer Chicago-area historic cemetery to Burr Oak Cemetery (CTL-E-1225).

name: Odell Beckham Jr.
description: Odell Beckham Jr., born 5 November 1992 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, is an American football wide receiver whose one-handed touchdown catch against Dallas on 23 November 2014 became one of the most replayed plays in NFL history. He attended Isidore Newman School in New Orleans and played at LSU before the New York Giants selected him 12th overall in the 2014 NFL Draft. Despite missing the first four games of his rookie season he caught 91 passes for 1,305 yards and 12 touchdowns and was named NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year; across five seasons in New York he totaled 390 receptions for 5,476 yards and 44 touchdowns. Traded to Cleveland in 2019, he later joined the Los Angeles Rams during the 2021 season, scored the opening touchdown of Super Bowl LVI, and tore his ACL in the same game as the Rams won the championship. After seasons with Baltimore in 2023 and Miami in 2024, a brief 2026 return to the Giants ended with his release on 29 September 2026, and the Minnesota Vikings then signed him to their practice squad.

name: Oscar Charleston
description: Oscar Charleston (1896–1954) is regarded by many historians as the greatest all-around player in Negro leagues history; in 2001 Bill James ranked him the fourth-greatest player of all time, behind only Ruth, Wagner, and Mays. An Indianapolis native, Charleston enlisted in the Army at fifteen, starred for the segregated 24th Infantry's team in the Philippines, and came home in 1915 to the Indianapolis ABCs, beginning a career of nearly four decades as player, player-manager, scout, and umpire. A center fielder who played shallow and ran down drives, a feared slugger, and the Negro leagues' all-time stolen-base leader in the surviving record, he starred for the ABCs, Chicago American Giants, Harrisburg Giants, Hilldale, Homestead Grays, and, as player-manager from 1932, the Pittsburgh Crawfords of Gibson and Paige. He and Josh Gibson share the record of three Negro league batting titles, and he is now credited with three Triple Crowns. Charleston later scouted for Branch Rickey — his recommendation helped bring Roy Campanella to the Dodgers' organization — and managed the Indianapolis Clowns to a pennant in 1954, weeks before his death in Philadelphia that October. He was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1976.

name: Olandria Carthen
description: Olandria Lashae Carthen, born 29 May 1998 in Decatur, Alabama, is an American model, influencer and television personality. A first-generation college graduate, she earned a bachelor's degree in logistics, materials and supply chain management from Tuskegee University and worked as an elevator and escalator sales specialist for Otis Elevator Company. In June 2025 she entered the villa as an original Islander on the seventh season of Peacock's Love Island USA, coupled finally with Nicolas Vansteenberghe, and finished as a runner-up. Known to fans as the Bama Barbie, she won the fan-voted People's Choice Award at the 2025 EBONY Power 100, and made her Sports Illustrated Swimsuit debut as a rookie in the magazine's 2026 issue. She attended the 2026 BET Awards in June 2026, and People reported in July 2026 that she and Vansteenberghe had parted ways.

name: Oscar Joyo
description: Oscar Joyo is a Malawian-born, Chicago-based visual artist — painter, illustrator, digital artist and muralist — whose work mixes Afrofuturism and Afrosurrealism. The University of Illinois Center for Advanced Study hosted him as a GAM Visiting Artist, with a lecture on February 26, 2026, and he created a mural for the Champaign County African American Heritage Trail; his work has been shown at Chicago galleries including Vertical Gallery. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
